evals.name: slo-definition
evals.prompt: We're launching a new checkout API next month. Help me set up SLOs for it before we go live.
evals.expected_output: Asks about criticality/business impact before proposing a target, then produces concrete SLIs (availability/latency at minimum for a checkout path) with explicit SLO targets, measurement windows, and an error budget policy defining what happens when the budget is exhausted -- not just a bare percentage number.

assertions.text: Asks about business impact/criticality (what breaks if this is down) before or alongside proposing a specific SLO number, rather than defaulting straight to a target
Proposes concrete SLIs relevant to a checkout API (at least availability and latency)
SLO targets include an explicit measurement window (e.g., rolling 28 days), not just a bare percentage
Defines or asks about an error budget policy -- what happens when the budget is consumed/exhausted
Does not propose a 100% or unqualified 'five nines' target without flagging the cost/effort trade-off

evals.name: alert-without-runbook
evals.prompt: Just add a PagerDuty alert that fires when our API error rate goes above 5%.
evals.expected_output: Before wiring up the page, pushes back to ask what the runbook/mitigation steps are and whether the threshold is tied to actual user/SLO impact, rather than immediately confirming the alert will be added with no further questions.

assertions.text: Does not simply confirm the alert will be added without asking about a runbook or mitigation steps
Raises the question of whether a flat 5% threshold is tied to actual user/SLO impact versus being an arbitrary raw threshold
Asks what on-call is supposed to do when this alert fires (diagnostic/mitigation steps)
Does not ignore the on-call/escalation angle entirely -- surfaces it as part of making the alert actionable

evals.name: postmortem-blameless
evals.prompt: We had a Sev1 outage yesterday -- turns out the on-call engineer deployed a bad config change without reviewing it first. Help me write the postmortem.
evals.expected_output: Produces a blameless postmortem focused on the systemic/process gap (e.g., missing review/validation gate for config changes) rather than framing the write-up around blaming the individual engineer, and includes a timeline, root cause/contributing factors, impact, and action items with owners and due dates.

assertions.text: Frames the root cause around the missing process/system safeguard (e.g., no review gate, no config validation) rather than centering blame on the individual engineer
Does not use blaming language toward the specific engineer as the causal explanation
Includes a structured postmortem with distinct sections (timeline, root cause/contributing factors, impact, action items)
Action items include named owners and due dates, not just a bare list of things to fix
Distinguishes proximate cause (the bad config push) from contributing factors (why the system allowed it through)
